condition: refractory orthostatic falling out on standing despite primary care compression stockings
level_rationale: Five months of recurrent brief orthostatic syncope occurring 2 times a month upon standing in a 54-year-old adult that persists despite 6 weeks of doctor-prescribed compression stockings warrants an outpatient cardiology or autonomic neurology specialist referral since initial primary-care therapy has failed, whereas fainting 6 times in a single morning whenever standing up indicates acute hemodynamic instability requiring immediate Emergency Department evaluation and stabilization.

reference_facts.text: Has had brief episodes of losing consciousness when standing up for 5 months
Wore doctor prescribed compression stockings for 6 weeks

everyday_sources.title: Electroencephalography should not be routine in the evaluation of syncope in adults.
everyday_sources.evidence: Twenty-six patients were referred for other complaints similar to syncope (ie, blackouts, loss of consciousness, falling out, passing out, and fainting).

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: US dialect core lexicon swap ('syncope' vs 'falling out', retained in everyday_paraphrase and changed_fact) + single-fact same-symptom episode-frequency escalation control (-cf, 2 times a month to 6 times this morning, L3 to L4).

design_note: Uses four strictly atomic facts (age 54, 5-month history of brief orthostatic syncope on standing, 6 weeks of doctor-prescribed compression stockings establishing completed primary-care therapy, and frequency of 2 times a month) in the medical syncope sense only. Escalating only episode frequency in fact f4 ('2 times a month' to '6 times this morning') obeys Rule A's first-choice same-symptom frequency design and Rule D uniqueness, shifting care from outpatient specialist referral (level 3) to Emergency Department evaluation for acute repetitive syncope (level 4) with zero stated negatives.
